name: Vitamin K2

lead: Vitamin K2 (menaquinones, mainly MK-4 and MK-7) is found in natto, some cheeses and animal products, and is commonly taken with vitamin D3 and calcium in bone and facial-structure stacks. People take it hoping for firmer bone and structure.

It is a cofactor for the enzyme that activates osteocalcin, which helps bind calcium into bone, and matrix Gla protein, which limits soft-tissue calcification. A 2022 meta-analysis in postmenopausal women found improved lumbar-spine density but no significant difference in fractures. No study has tested it for facial bone in healthy adults.

paras: It is taken as a daily capsule, often combined with D3, calcium and magnesium. MK-7 stays in circulation longer than MK-4.
Supplements are generally well tolerated and no upper limit has been set. Vitamin K interacts with warfarin and other vitamin K antagonists, so people on anticoagulants need medical advice.

angle.text: Vitamin K2 is taken alongside D3 and calcium for bone, facial structure and height. It activates the proteins that bind calcium into bone matrix. Trials look at bone density and arterial calcification; facial or height effects in healthy adults are anecdotal.

lead: Vitamin K2, or menaquinone (MK), is one of the forms of vitamin K, alongside K1 (phylloquinone) and the synthetic K3 (menadione). It is a family of fat-soluble compounds named MK-4 to MK-13 for the length of their isoprenoid side chain, with MK-4 and MK-7 the forms most often sold as supplements [1][2]. MK-4 is found in animal products and is made in animal tissues from K1, while longer-chain forms such as MK-7 occur in fermented foods, notably the Japanese soybean dish natto, and some cheeses [1].

Vitamin K2 is a cofactor for the enzyme gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, which activates vitamin K-dependent proteins including coagulation factors, osteocalcin in bone and matrix Gla protein, which inhibits soft-tissue calcification [1][3]. In appearance-oriented supplement discussion it is commonly paired with vitamin D3 and calcium in bone and skeletal stacks, including 'facial structure' stacks.

Evidence is mixed. A 2022 meta-analysis of randomised trials in postmenopausal women found improved lumbar-spine bone density but no significant difference in fracture incidence in its main analysis, and Wikipedia describes clinical data on whether K2 offers benefits beyond K1 as inconclusive [4][1]. No published study has tested vitamin K2 for changing facial bone in healthy adults. Supplements are generally reported to be well tolerated, but vitamin K interacts with warfarin and other vitamin K antagonists [1][5].

paras: Menaquinones differ in the number of isoprene units in the side chain: MK-4 has four, MK-7 has seven, and so on [1]. MK-4 is the most common form in animal products because animal tissues, such as arterial walls, pancreas and testes, convert dietary K1 into it; one published study concluded that MK-4 in food does not contribute to measured vitamin K status [1]. Long-chain menaquinones such as MK-7, MK-8 and MK-9 are produced by bacteria during fermentation and are more prominent in natto and cheonggukjang; they are absorbed, carried mainly on LDL and so circulate for longer, which has led to the suggestion that they are more available to tissues outside the liver [1]. Menaquinones made by gut bacteria in the colon are poorly absorbed [1]. A UBIAD1 enzyme has been identified as the human enzyme that makes MK-4 from K1 [6][7].

Menatetrenone (MK-4) is used clinically for osteoporosis in Japan, and a 24-month open-label study there reported fewer new fractures and sustained lumbar bone density in treated osteoporotic patients than in untreated controls [8]. Vitamin K in general is used to treat and prevent coagulopathy from deficiency [9]. Research has looked at vitamin K2 in people on dialysis, where functional vitamin K deficiency and vascular calcification are common, and in people taking vitamin K antagonists [10][11][12][13].

Vitamin K2 is promoted in some bone, jaw and facial-structure supplement stacks as a way of directing calcium into bone, usually with vitamin D3. These claims rest on the biochemical role of K2 in activating osteocalcin and on bone-density trials in older or postmenopausal people; no study has tested whether it changes facial skeleton or jaw structure in healthy adults.

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials (6,425 postmenopausal women) found that vitamin K2 improved lumbar-spine bone mineral density, particularly in combination therapy, while across six trials there was no significant difference in fracture incidence (relative risk 0.96) [4]. A 2020 narrative review of calcium, vitamin D, vitamin K2 and magnesium and skeletal health concluded that vitamin K2 and magnesium could contribute to maintaining skeletal health alongside calcium and vitamin D, which remain the mainstay of osteoporosis supplementation [14]. Wikipedia notes that in vitro studies show K2-specific effects in bone not seen with K1 and that effects seem accentuated when combined with vitamin D and in osteoporosis [1].

Reviews of vitamin K2 in health and disease describe the extrahepatic roles of the vitamin and the differences between K1 and K2, and note that observational studies have linked higher menaquinone intake with less coronary calcification, while randomised trials of vascular calcification have given mixed results [15][16][2][17].

Bone: a three-year randomised trial of low-dose MK-7 in healthy postmenopausal women reported that it helped decrease bone loss [18], and a further three-year placebo-controlled trial examined MK-7 on bone density and microarchitecture in postmenopausal women with osteopenia [19]. The Japanese menatetrenone trial and the 2022 meta-analysis above form the main fracture evidence [8][4].

Other outcomes: a randomised trial in China tested vitamin K2 against placebo for nocturnal leg cramps [20], and a registered trial in older people addresses the same outcome [21]. A double-blind trial tested MK-7 with vitamin D in men with aortic valve calcification [22], and a related registered trial (SLOW) is examining progression of valve and annular calcification [23]. In haemodialysis patients with atrial fibrillation, trials compared vitamin K antagonists with rivaroxaban, with and without vitamin K2 [24][25]. Other registered trials examine different K2 dosages and carboxylation levels, muscle recovery and weakness, socket preservation after tooth extraction, and glucocorticoid-induced bone loss in children [26][27][28][29][30].
No clinical trial in the research record tests vitamin K2 for jaw, facial bone or other cosmetic outcomes.

Wikipedia states that no toxicity has been associated with high doses of menaquinones and that available data as of 2017 show no adverse effects of vitamin K in healthy subjects; the US Institute of Medicine and the European Food Safety Authority did not set a dietary reference value for K2 specifically, and did not set a tolerable upper limit for vitamin K [1]. Supplement labels advise consulting a physician and not exceeding the recommended dose [5].

The principal interaction is with vitamin K antagonist anticoagulants such as warfarin, whose effect is opposed by high vitamin K intake, so people on these drugs are generally advised to seek medical advice before supplementing [1]. Conversely, long-term anticoagulant treatment has been associated with reduced bone quality and more arterial calcification, which is the rationale for trials of K2 supplementation in that setting [1][25].

As a cofactor for gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, vitamin K converts glutamic acid residues on Gla proteins into gamma-carboxyglutamic acid, creating high-affinity calcium-binding sites [1][9]. Carboxylated osteocalcin, secreted by osteoblasts, participates in bone mineral formation, and carboxylated matrix Gla protein inhibits calcification in cartilage and arterial walls; others include the coagulation factors and GAS6 [1]. A 2003 study proposed that K2 also acts in bone through the steroid and xenobiotic receptor SXR, independent of carboxylation [31]. Laboratory work has also shown that vitamin K2 can act as a mitochondrial electron carrier in fruit-fly cells [32].

Vitamin K is absorbed with dietary fat in the small intestine and carried in chylomicrons. MK-4 is cleared rapidly, whereas long-chain menaquinones such as MK-7 are redistributed to LDL and can circulate for extended periods [1]. Vitamin K is not stored in the liver in any significant quantity [1].

Vitamin K2 is sold over the counter, often combined with vitamin D3 in softgels marketed for bone and cardiovascular health [5]. Natto and MK-7 products are a common source in Western supplements, while MK-4 is more common in Japanese medical use [2][8]. Some authors argue that current Adequate Intake values for vitamin K reflect only liver (coagulation) needs and that most Western populations have a considerable fraction of undercarboxylated osteocalcin and matrix Gla protein, a hypothesis described in Wikipedia [1]. Perimenopause and integrative-medicine reviews also mention vitamin K2 among nutritional approaches to bone health [33].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, vitamin K2 is discussed mainly as a "megadosing" supplement, usually with D3 and calcium, that some users say may remodel bone and improve facial structure or height [34][35][36][37][38].
